::: {.why}
Calendar effects are the easiest patterns to find, the hardest to distinguish from noise, and the ones with the weakest reason to persist, which makes them the ideal drill for the discipline you have been building.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Compute the number of calendar hypotheses available in a return series, and the best result you would expect under the null.
- State the standard you would require before trading a calendar effect, and check whether any of yours meets it.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Count the hypotheses: months, days of week, days of month, turn of month, holidays, and the interactions of these with sub-universes. Then run the whole grid on your data and record the best t-statistic. Then run the identical grid on 200 synthetic series from qlib.simulate and report the distribution of the best t-statistic under the null. Your real best will probably sit inside that distribution.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Write the standard: a calendar effect needs a mechanism, out-of-sample persistence after publication, and presence in a second market, and almost none of them have all three. Then check the one or two that are most often cited in your own data with the corrected threshold applied.
:::
:::
